**In Defense of Getting Lost**

Every child knows two kinds of lost. There is the bad kind—the supermarket aisle where your mother's face has vanished, the sudden cold geometry of adult legs moving past—and there is the other kind, found at the end of a creek followed behind the houses until the backyards give way to trees and you look up and cannot name any street at all. The first kind teaches caution. The second, if you are lucky enough to survive it unremarked, teaches something stranger: that the world continues past the edge of the map you were handed, that you can find your way home, and that not knowing—briefly, safely endured—is nearer to wonder than to terror.

Then we grow up and set about losing nothing. We carry objects that know where we are to within a few meters, that announce turns before we need them, that can summon a picture of any corner of any city on earth. This is presented to us as freedom, and in many ways it is. But notice what else it is: the end of a certain education. For nearly all of human history, every journey contained a small wilderness of uncertainty. You might take a wrong turn. You might misjudge the distance. You might arrive somewhere you did not intend and have to negotiate with reality to get where you were going. That negotiation was a skill, and like all skills it was built through use.

People have always sensed this, which is why the great traditions of walking are also traditions of deliberate confusion. The flâneurs of nineteenth-century Paris strolled without destination precisely because destination was the enemy of seeing. The Situationists later gave the practice a name—the dérive, the drift—and treated it as a serious method, a way of letting the city speak instead of merely using it. Pilgrims walked for months toward distant shrines, but everyone understood the shrine was half the point; the other half was the long corridor of days in which a traveler could become someone slightly different than the one who set out. Even Thoreau admitted he sometimes stayed out past dark because his walks had carried him somewhere unplanned—and he suspected, rightly, that the best part of his day happened while lost.

What the blue dot took from us was not safety—we are safer—but the productive friction of being briefly wrong. Watch people navigate now: the phone speaks, the body obeys, and the mind is free to drift elsewhere entirely. We arrive having gone nowhere in the sense that matters. Compare this to navigating by folded paper map, an instrument that required you to hold the whole territory in your head at once—to know the museum is behind you and the river ahead, that north hangs over your left shoulder. With one, you built a model of the city inside yourself. You became a little map. And when a closed road forced you into unfamiliar blocks, you had the resources to improvise, and the improvisation left marks. People remember the streets they got lost in. Nobody remembers the streets they were routed through.

Something notable also happens in the mind during disorientation. When you know exactly where you are and what comes next, attention relaxes into shorthand; the world arrives pre-labeled. But when you are lost, attention snaps open. Every façade becomes information. Every signpost is read with the urgency of scripture. Researchers studying wayfinding find that people form richer memories of places navigated unaided, and anyone learning a new city knows it is true at the level of feeling: the streets you struggled through are the ones you own. Disorientation is a powerful teacher precisely because it refuses to summarize. It makes you do the work of orienting yourself, and the work is the lesson.

None of this needs to stay literal. We get lost in books, in arguments, in other people's troubles, in a problem of our own that swallows an afternoon. Intellectual lostness wears the same double face as the geographic kind: frustration braided with fascination. The mathematician stuck on a proof, the writer staring at a sentence that won't behave, the child dismantling a clock—they are all off the map, doing what experts call exploration when it succeeds and flailing when it doesn't. But every map of a field worth caring about was drawn by people willing to flail. Certainty is comfortable, and comfort is where curiosity goes to die. If you always know exactly where you stand in an idea, you are probably standing at its entrance, reading the plaque.

Still, it matters to distinguish getting lost from mere aimlessness, because they are not the same. Drifting can be lovely, but true lostness requires that you cared where you were going—that there was a destination, a plan, a self you expected to keep intact—and that reality disagreed. Lostness is what happens to intention when it collides with the world. This is why the word carries such weight beyond geography: people describe themselves as lost after a failure, a move, a heartbreak. We treat that state as purely negative, yet it is often the precondition for the next version of a life. You cannot reorient until you admit you are facing the wrong way. The admission hurts. It is also, quietly, hopeful—it means movement is still possible.

So consider, sometime soon, a small experiment. Leave the phone in your pocket—not off, just unprompted—and choose a direction you've never taken out of your own neighborhood, or walk your usual route backward, or follow the sound of water. Expect the flicker of anxiety; let it pass through you like weather. Notice how sharply the world arranges itself around your uncertainty, how much there is to see once seeing becomes necessary. Then find your way home by whatever means remain: the angle of the sun, the slope of the land, the kindness of a stranger. You will arrive late, slightly rumpled, with dirt on your shoes and a story nobody asked for. And for an hour or so, you will have been the author of your own route again—present in the world, finally, because you were lost enough to truly pay attention.

# Where the Voices Go

Every word spoken by a human being before 1860 is gone. Not merely forgotten—unrecoverable. This isn't poetry; it's physics. Socrates taught entirely by talking, and everything we know of his voice arrives secondhand, filtered through Plato's pen. Cleopatra spoke and nothing remains. Shakespeare never once read his own lines aloud into anything that could hold them. For nearly the whole span of human history, sound was the most perishable thing we made—a sentence existed for exactly as long as its vibrations took to fade from the air, and then it was annihilated as thoroughly as if it had never been spoken. The past, acoustically speaking, is a silent film with the reel missing.

Then, in 1857, a Parisian typesetter and amateur inventor named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville patented a strange machine: the phonautograph. A funnel gathered sound onto a flexible membrane, a boar's-bristle stylus rode the membrane's trembling, and the stylus scratched a wavy line of soot onto paper rolled beneath it. Here's the haunting part—Scott never intended to play his recordings back. He couldn't. He wanted to *study* sound visually, the way a botanist presses a flower. On April 9, 1860, someone sang "Au Clair de la Lune" into his funnel, and the melody became a squiggle in lampblack. Nearly a hundred and fifty years later, physicists at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory scanned that soot line with a light-sensitive instrument designed to read old data tapes, converted the wobble into a waveform—and a voice rose out of the nineteenth century. Ten seconds long, warbling, unmistakably human. It predates Edison's phonograph by seventeen years. Whoever that singer was—and it was very likely Scott himself—he died in 1879, and in 2008, people heard him breathe.

Sit with the strangeness of that: a recording made by a man who knew it could never be heard, preserved in a form meant only for eyes, waiting a century and a half for someone to build the ear. It's like finding a letter written in a language its author hoped someone would someday invent.

But the story curdles from there, because we learned to keep sounds at almost precisely the moment the world began losing them. Consider the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō, a small, glossy Hawaiian bird with a fluted, bell-like song. Mosquitoes carrying avian malaria crept up the islands' slopes, and the ʻōʻō retreated higher and higher into the mountain forests until, by the 1980s, only a handful remained—then one. A single male. In 1987, biologists recorded him singing. His species' song was a duet, male and female parts woven together, and he sang all of it—the courtship phrases, the answering phrases—performed both halves flawlessly to a mate who would never come. He was calling into an emptiness that had swallowed everyone who might have replied. He was never seen again. The recording survives in an archive at Cornell. You can listen to an entire species' final voice, and it is a love song with no one on the other side.

Or consider the whale. In 1989, U.S. Navy hydrophone arrays—built, ironically, to listen for submarines—picked up a call in the North Pacific unlike any other: a pattern resembling blue or fin whale song, but pitched around 52 hertz, far higher than either species typically calls. Researchers at Woods Hole tracked this single animal for years as it swam thousands of miles. Its voice matched no known population. Somewhere in that vast ocean was, apparently, one whale calling at a frequency its own kind might not hear—a creature nicknamed "the loneliest whale in the world," though the scientist who studied it gently warned against projecting our ache onto what may be a perfectly content hybrid or oddball. Perhaps. It's hard not to imagine it singing and singing into water that gives nothing back.

The bioacoustician Bernie Krause has spent decades recording wild soundscapes, sorting the world's audio into what he calls biophony (all living sound), geophony (wind, rain, rivers), and anthropophony (us). His archive contains a devastating experiment in time: he returns, year after year, to places he taped in the 1960s, 70s, and 80s. At Lincoln Meadow in the Sierra Nevada, he recorded before and after a selective logging operation. Photographs show almost no difference. The trees are there; the meadow is green. But the soundscape collapsed—fewer birds, thinner layers, gaps in the dawn chorus where there had once been dense, interlocking music. His conclusion after a lifetime of this work: habitats can look intact while sounding empty. He estimates that roughly half of what he captured can no longer be heard in the places where he captured it.

And so the irony completes itself. We built machines to preserve sound just as we set about flooding the world with noise we'd rather forget. Shipping lanes grow louder year by year, and whales near busy ports go quiet or raise their voices just to be heard over our propellers. The quietest places on the continent are overflown by aircraft dozens of times a day. True quiet—quiet with texture and life in it—is becoming as scarce as dark night sky.

Yet there is another way to hold all this, and it's gentler. Every conversation you have today will vanish too, joining Socrates' lectures in the great acoustic void, unless someone switches on a recorder. Which means that listening remains one of the last perishable acts we perform. To truly attend to a friend's voice, or rain on a roof, is to receive something that cannot be archived—and perhaps that ephemerality was always the point. Music matters because it dies into silence. Attention matters because it cannot be saved.

Scott de Martinville gave us permanence. But the universe spent billions of years filling itself with sound—thunder, whale song, the drumming of rain—with no one there to hear it, and now, for a brief window, there are ears everywhere. So tonight, stop for ten seconds, the length of that first scratchy recording, and listen to one small thing: the refrigerator's hum, wind finding a window frame, a moth tapping glass. Almost nothing that has ever been heard left a trace. You're part of the brief miracle of hearing anyway. Listen while it lasts.

# In Defense of Darkness

Try to remember the last time you experienced true darkness. Not the dimness of a bedroom with curtains drawn, not the amber hush of a city street at 3 a.m., but genuine darkness — the kind that erases your own hand when you hold it up before your face. For most of us, such moments are vanishingly rare. We live inside a permanent twilight of our own making, a glow that leaks upward from every streetlamp, billboard, and window until even the night itself has been domesticated.

Astronomers have a name for the result: light pollution. By their estimates, more than eighty percent of North Americans can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Globally, roughly a third of humanity — and nearly everyone in Europe and the United States — has lost sight of the galaxy we inhabit. Think about that: the great river of stars that every human who ever lived gazed upon, until about a century ago, is now a rumor, something you must travel to remote deserts and mountaintops to verify.

This is a strange thing to have lost, and stranger still that we barely noticed losing it. For nearly all of human history, night was a genuine frontier. When the sun went down, firelight made only a small island in the dark, and beyond its edge stretched a world belonging to the moon and stars. Those lights weren't decoration; they were infrastructure. Farmers read the seasons in them. Sailors steered by them. The stars told Polynesian navigators when to set out across open ocean; the heliacal rising of Sirius told Egyptian priests that the Nile would soon flood. And because there was little else to do in those long hours, the sky became our first cinema and our first scripture — every culture projecting its heroes, beasts, and gods onto those flickering points, telling stories across the fire about why the world was as it was.

Electric light gave us enormous gifts. It extended the working day, made streets safer, opened the night to reading, medicine, conversation. But like many gifts, it arrived quietly bundled with a cost nobody itemized. We didn't just illuminate the night; we displaced it. And displacement has consequences that reach far beyond nostalgia.

Consider first the body. Human physiology was tuned over hundreds of thousands of years to a planet that turned reliably between light and dark. Darkness triggers the release of melatonin, the hormone that governs sleep; the blue-white glare of screens and LEDs suppresses it. Chronic exposure to light at night scrambles our circadian rhythms, and through them, our health. We are, quite literally, built for a daily passage into darkness, and we keep canceling the trip.

Then consider the creatures whose lives depend on the dark. On beaches from Florida to Oman, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant the moonlit sea. Now they crawl toward beachfront hotels and perish in parking lots. Migrating birds, navigating by stars they can no longer see, circle illuminated skyscrapers in confusion, dying by the hundreds of millions each year in collisions. Insects — moths especially, those devoted servants of the moon — spiral exhausted around our porch lamps. Whole ecosystems dim when the night does.

And yet the loss isn't merely biological. Something in us needed the dark, too. When Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* in 1889 from the window of his asylum in Saint-Rémy, he was working from memory and longing as much as observation — but the cypress tree and the swirling sky belong to a world where night still had a face. The Romantics walked out into it deliberately, seeking in darkness what daylight couldn't provide: awe, smallness, communion with something larger than themselves. Night was where imagination went to stretch.

There is a particular kind of thinking that happens only in the dark. With vision — our dominant sense — dialed down, attention turns inward. The dark removes surfaces and leaves essence. It is no accident that we associate it with both fear and intimacy: with monsters under the bed and with whispered conversations late into the night. The fear is ancient and honest; our ancestors had real reasons to dread what they couldn't see. But the other inheritance is just as old — darkness as shelter, as rest, as the great leveler where everything exposed in daylight grows equal and quiet.

A few places are trying to hand it back. There are now certified International Dark Sky Reserves — in Utah's canyon country, in New Zealand's Mackenzie Basin, on remote Atlantic islands — where local ordinances forbid excess lighting and visitors can once again lie on their backs beneath an unbroken bowl of stars. First-timers often expect the postcard version: blazing constellations on black velvet. What they actually get is subtler and stranger. Under a truly dark sky, the Milky Way doesn't shine so much as haunt — a pale, luminous rift overhead, so faint and so vast that newcomers sometimes mistake it for a cloud. Then the adjustment comes, and with it a quiet vertigo: the cloud is made of some two hundred billion suns, and we are looking at it from the inside.

Here is the deeper argument underneath all of this: a species that abolishes darkness may eventually forget what darkness is for. Light means knowledge, clarity, productivity, exposure — all fine things. But darkness is the necessary complement: rest, mystery, patience, the willingness not to know. A culture lit twenty-four hours a day begins to believe that everything worth seeing is already visible, that every question deserves an instant answer, that there is no proper time for anything except now. The dark sky argues otherwise. It rewards those who wait — twenty minutes, half an hour — while their eyes slowly reopen capacities they didn't know they had closed.

So consider this an invitation. Some clear, moonless night, walk to wherever the streetlights end. Switch off your flashlight and stand still. Let your eyes adjust; it takes longer than you think. Then look up and meet the one darkness we have left — the original one, older than fire, patient enough to wait for us to come back.

# The Door Left Open

In 1822, twenty-five-year-old Franz Schubert wrote two movements of a symphony and set down his pen. He sketched part of a third—a scherzo that peters out mid-page—and then nothing more. He never returned to it. He never destroyed it either. He simply passed the manuscript to a friend, and there it sat in a drawer for forty years, unseen and unheard. When it was finally performed in Vienna in 1865, long after Schubert had died at thirty-one, listeners recognized it at once as a masterpiece. It has carried the name "Unfinished Symphony" ever since, as though the label were an apology. But hear it for yourself: two movements of such dark, luminous wholeness that the missing third and fourth feel less like failure than like a door left open on purpose.

No one knows why he stopped. Illness, some say—he was diagnosed with syphilis that year, and depression followed him like a shadow afterward. Others blame a dissolved commission or simple despair. My favorite theory is the least dramatic: he said what needed saying in two movements, and the rest would have been commentary.

We are uneasy around unfinished things, and drawn to them, often in the same breath. Consider Michelangelo's *Slaves* in Florence—four figures abandoned rough-hewn, bodies straining to free themselves from the marble, souls caught mid-waking inside stone. Many visitors find them more moving than his polished masterpieces, precisely because you witness creation itself frozen mid-struggle: becoming rather than being. Leonardo da Vinci left behind fewer completed paintings than almost any artist of his stature, canvases halted in ghostly underpainting, and somehow this makes him larger, not smaller—an imagination too fast for its own hands.

Literature is a museum of glorious fragments. Coleridge dreamed *Kubla Khan* entire, began transcribing, was interrupted by a man from Porlock, and lost the rest forever; the poem remains one of the most famous in English, though by his own account it was merely a shard of something greater. Kafka died in a sanatorium in 1924 having ordered his friend Max Brod to burn every unpublished page. Brod refused. Because of that single act of disobedience we have *The Trial* and *The Castle*—novels that break off mid-sentence yet feel eerily complete, as if Kafka understood that ending things honestly was impossible and chose not to pretend otherwise.

And then there is Barcelona, where the Sagrada Família has been under construction since 1882. Antoni Gaudí devoted the last decades of his life to it, lived like a pauper inside the workshop, and was killed in 1926 by a streetcar, mistaken at first for a beggar. Asked about the glacial pace of construction, he reportedly shrugged: "My client is not in a hurry." Nearly a century and a half later, cranes still lean over the towers, and generations of architects have inherited not a blueprint but a question.

Psychology has noticed our strange attachment to the incomplete. In the 1920s, the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik heard Kurt Lewin remark that waiters in a café could remember complicated unpaid orders perfectly—until the bill was settled, at which point the memory seemed to evaporate. Her experiments confirmed the pattern: interrupted tasks stick in the mind measurably better than finished ones. The mind keeps a hand on what remains open. Unfinished things stay warm.

Everyone owns a drawer of unfinished things, literal or otherwise: half a novel, a letter drafted and never sent, a scarf missing its final rows, a language learned up to the plateau of halting conversation and then abandoned. Why do we keep these relics instead of throwing them away? I suspect it's because an unfinished thing is still possible. Once finished, a project becomes one fixed answer—it is whatever it turned out to be. Unfinished, it contains every answer it might have had. The half-novel can still be brilliant. The moment you type *The End*, it becomes merely what it is.

Modern productivity culture treats unfinishedness as debt. Close your loops. Ship it. Done is better than perfect. There's real wisdom here—someone who begins a hundred projects and completes none is usually evading the hard part, the part where the thing pushes back. But there's a loss hiding in the slogan too. Completion is a kind of burial. To finish something entirely is to stop listening to it, to seal it off from further thought, the way a verdict seals off a case. Some of the best relationships we have—with books, places, ideas—are the ones we've never fully resolved.

Besides, nearly everything important stays unfinished whether we like it or not. Conversations severed mid-sentence by arriving trains. Friendships that faded without argument or farewell, so that years later you're unsure whether they ended or merely paused. Griefs that soften but refuse to conclude. Questions carried for decades without answers, growing familiar as old furniture. "Closure" is mostly a story we assemble afterward, tidying the past into plots. What life actually provides are pauses.

Which brings us back to Schubert. Conductors have proposed completions; scholars still hunt for a vanished finale. But audiences keep returning to the version where the music simply stops—where the second movement fades and the concert hall holds its collective breath for a third movement that will never arrive. In that held breath, every listener composes a small piece of the missing symphony alone. Perhaps that is what unfinished things are ultimately for. They recruit us. They hand us the pen.

So keep one thing deliberately undone. Not out of laziness—out of hospitality. Leave a project hovering, a letter unsent, a question unanswered, a door ajar somewhere in the house of your life. Let the draft blow through. Whatever is still open can still surprise you; whatever is still possible cannot yet disappoint. Schubert put down his pen and walked away, and in doing so gave the world two perfect movements plus a silence—and the silence, it turns out, belongs to us.

# On Writing in the Margins

There's a small pleasure known to anyone who buys used books: you reach page 117 of a secondhand novel and discover, in faded ballpoint, a stranger's verdict — *no, he wouldn't say this.* Suddenly you are not reading alone. The book now contains two voices: the author's and some vanished reader's, locked in argument across the decades while you eavesdrop from the couch.

We tend to treat books as sacred objects. Children are scolded for scribbling in them, libraries levy fines against defacement, and there's a certain person at every dinner party who winces at the sight of a dog-eared page. The instinct isn't wrong — a marked-up book is a diminished commodity. But the urge to annotate is older than the rule against it, older than print itself, and considerably more interesting than the etiquette suppressing it.

The patron saint of the practice is Samuel Taylor Coleridge, who scribbled so prolifically in other people's books that lending him a volume became a calculated gamble. His friends learned to hand over books half-hoping to get them back annotated, because Coleridge's margins were sometimes better than the text they surrounded — a running commentary from one of the great minds of the age, delivered in the white space between printed lines. He took the habit seriously enough to name it, importing the mock-scholarly Latin *marginalia* into English and even sketching a taxonomy of the form. For Coleridge, the margin was not vandalism. It was a venue.

The tradition goes back much further. In medieval monasteries, where every book had to be copied by hand, scribes left messages in the margins that were less literary criticism than diary entries of suffering. Genuine ones survive: complaints about cold fingers, bad ink, dim lamplight, the ache in a bent back. At least one scribe, setting down his pen at last, signed off with what reads like pure relief — a plea, essentially, for someone to bring him a drink. These men weren't commenting on Aristotle. They were leaving proof of endurance. The manuscript happened to be the surface nearest to hand, the way a prisoner scratches tallies on a wall.

And occasionally a margin note doesn't just accompany history — it hijacks it. In 1637, Pierre de Fermat sketched a mathematical claim beside a problem in his copy of Diophantus's *Arithmetica* and added, with what must have been magnificent serenity, that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of it — but the margin was too narrow to contain it. Whether he actually possessed such a proof is doubted by nearly everyone now. What the note became instead was a taunt lasting three hundred and fifty years. Generations of mathematicians broke themselves against what came to be called Fermat's Last Theorem, until Andrew Wiles finally proved it in the 1990s using machinery Fermat could never have imagined. Three centuries of obsessive genius, all traceable to a single sentence squeezed beside a Greek text because there wasn't room below.

What drives the urge in its humbler forms? I think it's this: reading *feels* like conversation, but it's conversation with a mute partner. You laugh, you object, you want to shout *yes, exactly* — and the author cannot hear you. The margin is where the reply goes. It's a rehearsal of speech, a fossil record of a mind in motion. That's why even hostile marginalia can be strangely moving: you're watching thought happen, unedited, in real time. The printed text is finished, sealed, indifferent to centuries of opinion. The marginal note is still warm.

This is precisely what e-readers fail to capture, despite their best efforts. Your device will cheerfully inform you that "247 people have highlighted this passage," which is demographically interesting and spiritually dead. Aggregation flattens thousands of private reactions into a consensus bar chart. What disappears is the singular voice — the specific anonymous soul whose *!!!* beside a line of poetry conveys nothing statistically but everything personally. A margin note is a message from one individual to whoever happens next. Popular highlights are weather reports; marginalia is a letter.

Used bookstores are full of these small hauntings. The inscription: *To Margaret, all my love, Christmas 1974*, both parties now gone, the token of their affection priced at two dollars. The train ticket serving forever as a bookmark at a chapter someone apparently never reached. A phone number on the flyleaf, ten digits that once meant everything to somebody. A flattened flower pressing a page toward the end of a romance novel, placed there deliberately, by a hand that believed in the story enough to preserve a piece of the world inside it. Each artifact testifies that this book was not merely read. It was lived alongside.

Maybe that's the deepest reason to write in books, house rules be damned: it is evidence of presence. Silent reading leaves no trace. The eyes cross the page and depart without luggage. Ink is proof. Somewhere out there, right now, is a copy of *Middlemarch* carrying your grandmother's penciled objections, and if you ever find it, you will get thirty unscripted seconds of her thinking — her humor, her impatience, the exact shape of her mind at the moment Dorothea made her furious. No photograph does that. Photographs show you a face; marginalia shows you a consciousness.

So the next time a passage stops you cold, ignore the ghost of every librarian who ever frowned in your direction. Find a pen. Argue back. Underline furiously, draw your arrows, ask your questions into the empty white space. The author won't answer — authors never do, that's the deal — but someone in 2085, holding a yellowed paperback bought for a dollar at an estate sale, might stumble onto your furious little note and feel the sudden static of another mind touching theirs across the gap.

They'll realize, with a small shock of company, that they are not reading alone.

None of us ever were. That's what the margins are for.

**In Praise of Moss**

After a rain, look at any old stone wall, any cracked sidewalk, any shaded roof shingle. There it is: a low green nap pressed against the world, so familiar you've likely stopped seeing it. Moss is the wallpaper of the outdoors, the felt lining of forests, the soft failure of lawns. We walk over it without ceremony. But kneel down—actually get your knees wet—and you're looking at one of the strangest success stories life has ever produced.

Consider everything a moss doesn't have. No roots—it has rhizoids, hairlike anchors that hold on but barely drink. No vascular system, none of those internal straws that let trees hoist water two hundred feet skyward, which is why moss stays low and humble; it cannot afford height. No flowers. No seeds. No fruit, no pollen, no show. And yet it covers every continent, including Antarctica, thrives in deserts and tundra and city gutters, and was almost certainly among the first living things to crawl out of the water and take up residence on bare rock.

That last point deserves a moment of awe. Around 470 million years ago, long before trees existed, before insects, before anything we'd recognize as a landscape, ancestral relatives of moss began greening the land. There was nothing to stand on, really—no soil, just mineral grit. So these pioneers made soil themselves, secreting acids that broke stone into particles, trapping dust, dying and composting into the very ground other life would eventually need. Some scientists suspect they changed the climate too: pulling carbon dioxide from the air as they weathered rock, they may have helped chill the whole planet into an ancient ice age. The quietest organisms on Earth, rewriting the atmosphere. It's tempting to say they were unassuming. They were not unassuming. They were foundational.

Here's another trick, and it may be the best one. Most plants guard their hydration like treasure—wilt, and they're damaged; dry out entirely, and they die. Moss shrugs. Its water content simply matches the air around it. In drought it goes brown, brittle, seemingly dead, and waits—days, months, sometimes years—until water returns, at which point it rehydrates and resumes photosynthesis within minutes, as if nothing happened. Not survival exactly. More like suspension of the argument. Moss has opted out of the arms race altogether: instead of fighting scarcity, it simply steps aside from it and comes back when conditions improve. Botanists have revived moss frozen beneath Antarctic ice for perhaps fifteen centuries. Imagine a strategy so patient that death is just a pause button.

Then there is the empire-builder of the family, Sphagnum, the peat moss. A fistful of Sphagnum can absorb many times its weight in water—it once served as bandage dressing in field hospitals because it outperformed cotton. Across the cold latitudes of the world, Sphagnum builds bogs: waterlogged, acidic, oxygen-starved landscapes where decomposition nearly stops. Things fall in and stay. This is why we've recovered "bog bodies"—people preserved for thousands of years with skin, hair, even stomach contents intact, sunk in what amounts to a giant natural pickle jar. It's also why bogs matter enormously right now: peatlands cover only a few percent of the planet's land surface but hold a staggering share of its soil carbon, centuries of accumulated greenery that never fully rotted. Draining them releases what the moss spent millennia banking.

Kneel closer still. A single cushion of moss is not a plant; it's a habitat, a high-rise for the very small. Tardigrades—the famously indestructible "water bears"—graze the damp surfaces between leaflets. Rotifers wheel their spinning crowns through microscopic pools. Springtails, mites, nematodes, all packed into a green mound the size of a teacup. Press your ear to it if you like; you won't hear them, but you'll be leaning against a metropolis. Every patch of moss is an ecosystem folded small enough to overlook, which is precisely why it survives us.

We haven't always overlooked it, though. In Kyoto there's a temple famous for its moss—more than a hundred varieties carpeting the grounds in every texture of velvet. But here's the lovely part: the moss wasn't planned. The garden fell into disrepair, flooded, sat abandoned, and moss simply arrived, colonizing the neglect until the accident became the masterpiece. The temple now accepts visitors only by reservation, through a gate that requires written application—a pilgrimage to see what indifference accidentally grew. There's something instructive in that. Some of the most beautiful things humans have ever tended began as things we failed to tend.

So what does moss know that we don't? Perhaps this: that ambition is optional. Moss never competes for the canopy. It takes the leftovers—the shade nobody wants, the vertical surfaces nothing else can grip, the crumbs of moisture other plants would scorn—and it builds worlds there. It has survived five mass extinctions not by getting tougher but by getting flexible, mastering retreat and return. It does not grow tall, but it grows everywhere. It does not live fast, but it has outlived every empire, every dinosaur, every fashion.

And maybe the final lesson is about attention. Moss rewards proximity. From a standing height it's a smudge; from six inches away it's a forest of branching architecture, spore capsules rising like lanterns, dew strung along miniature lawns. The world is full of such places—systems running quietly at scales we weren't built to notice, holding up larger ones in ways we rarely credit. Soil beneath wheat. Bacteria in our guts. The unseen maintenance crews of existence.

The rain stops. The wall dries to a dull olive. Somewhere in that thin green crust, tardigrades curl up for the next dry spell, spores wait for wind, and half a billion years of patience continues its slow work of holding stones, storing carbon, softening the hard edges of the earth. All it asks is that occasionally, walking past, you look down.

# On Night Trains

The night train begins its work before you ever board it. You arrive at the station in that blue hour when the departure board has started listing tomorrow's trains beside today's, and already the world feels doubled—one foot in the day that's ending, one in the day that hasn't arrived. You find your carriage, wrestle your bag into a space designed by someone who clearly hated bags, and settle into a narrow berth that smells faintly of other people's journeys. Somewhere below, the engine is idling, patient, like a large animal that knows exactly when it intends to move.

Then comes the moment that no airplane can offer: the train pulls out of the station while you're still awake enough to feel it. Not the violent press of acceleration but a slow, almost apologetic slide. The platform lights begin to move—first gently, then faster—and then they're gone, and so is the station, and so is the city, and you are in motion without having done anything at all. You didn't take off. You were simply carried away. There is a difference, and the difference matters.

Sleeping while moving is one of the strangest bargains we've made with technology. Some ancient part of the brain refuses it outright—the body keeps flinching at every sway and clatter, convinced that movement at night means danger. And yet there we are, tucked under a thin railway blanket, surrendering consciousness inside a steel tube doing ninety kilometers an hour through the dark. It works only because of an elaborate web of trust: someone else is keeping watch. Signalmen, drivers, controllers scattered along a corridor of rails you will never see, all coordinating so that you can lie down and close your eyes. Sleep becomes a small act of faith in strangers.

And here is the finest trick the night train plays: it crosses borders while you sleep. You fall asleep in one country and wake in another. The fields outside the window have changed color overnight; the fences look different; the station names are suddenly spelled in letters you can't sound out. Nobody stamped anything. Nobody woke you. Geography, which seems so solid when you're standing in it, turns out to be negotiable if you simply agree to be unconscious through the seam. Waking up somewhere new without having traveled—having traveled precisely *by not witnessing*—feels like a permission slip from the world.

Then there are the fellow passengers, who exist only because of the train's peculiar geometry. In no other form of travel do you spend eight hours within arm's reach of people whose names you never learn. A student eating bread and cheese she bought at a kiosk. An old man who takes off his shoes immediately, unembarrassed, as though he's known you for years. Someone reading by a pinprick lamp long after everyone else has slept. You exchange nothing but glances and small courtesies—holding a door, passing down a ticket for checking—and yet by morning you share something real: you crossed the night together. The intimacy is brief and total and then, at the terminus, dissolved forever. It's friendship compressed into a single night and then released back into the atmosphere.

If the train has a dining car, dawn there is a kind of ceremony. Coffee that is objectively terrible tastes, in that context, like the best coffee on earth, because it arrives while the sun is coming up over scenery you have no context for—a river you can't name, a town with a smokestack and a church spire sliding past at eye level. The window frames everything like a film you wandered into mid-scene. You don't know the plot. You just know it's beautiful, and that your coffee is trembling very slightly in its cup from the motion, and that this tremble is somehow the point.

We tend to romanticize the great named expresses—the Orient Express, the Trans-Siberian—but the truth is that most night trains are gloriously ordinary, and their ordinariness is part of their dignity. They exist for nurses going home after a shift, for families visiting grandparents, for people for whom a hotel room is a luxury. The night train is one of the last pieces of infrastructure that treats distance as something to be *used* rather than merely endured. Why waste a day traveling when you can travel through the wasted hours anyway? The night was going to happen regardless. The train simply puts it to work.

This is what the airplane cannot forgive: it deletes distance. You rise above the earth, the earth becomes abstract, and three hours later you descend somewhere that might as well have been teleported into being. The night train insists that distance is real—that between here and there lie actual rivers, actual sleeping towns, actual weather. You feel the kilometers in your spine. You hear them in the couplings' rhythm, that hypnotic clack-clack... clack-clack, which is possibly the most honest sound humans have ever made: the sound of distance being paid off, installment by installment.

And there's a humbler lesson too. On a night train you are cargo that consents. Everything about your progress depends on systems and people you'll never meet—the maintenance crews grinding the wheels true, the dispatcher watching a wall of lights, the driver whose face you will never see, guiding two hundred tons of sleeping strangers through fog. We speak often of independence, but almost everything good in a human life runs on rails laid and tended by others. The night train makes this visible. You wake up safe in another country and understand, briefly, that you did nothing to deserve it except lie down and trust.

Then arrival: the brakes sing, the platform slides in, and you step off with that particular stiffness night trains give you—legs half-asleep, hair wrong, one sock missing—and the morning air of a new place hits you like cold water. You are exactly where you were headed, and you are subtly not the person who left. Nothing happened. That's the whole miracle. Nothing happened, all night, while everything moved.

Somewhere behind you the train waits a few minutes, exhaling, before backing out toward wherever trains go to rest. You carry the rhythm with you for days afterward—that soft double-beat in the chest, the body still believing, against all evidence, that it is being carried onward through the dark by hands it will never shake.

# The Color That Had to Be Mined

There is almost no real blue substance on Earth. That sounds absurd—blue is everywhere, the default color of distance—but nearly all the blue we see is borrowed from physics rather than chemistry. The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short wavelengths of light; the sea borrows the sky back. Living things rarely manufacture blue at all. Peacocks and morpho butterflies wear it through microscopic architecture, ridged surfaces that bend reflected light until our eyes read it as blue—grind a morpho's wing to powder and the blue vanishes, because there was never any blue in it, only geometry. True blue pigment, blue as matter, is one of the planet's rarest commodities. For most of human history it came from a single stone, pulled from a single valley in the mountains of Badakhshan, in northeastern Afghanistan.

The mines at Sar-e-Sang have been worked for some six thousand years, longer than most nations' entire recorded histories. High in the mountains, miners followed seams of marble in search of lapis lazuli—a rock the color of deep water, flecked with pyrite's false stars. Ground fine, its richest portions yield a powder more brilliant than the stone itself: the pigment Italians would call *ultramarino*, ultramarine, "beyond the sea," because it reached their ports—Venice above all—after the long crossing from the East.

Cennino Cennini, the Florentine painter whose craftsman's handbook appeared around 1400, called it "a color illustrious, beautiful, and most perfect beyond all other colors." His instructions for preparing it read like liturgy. The ground stone was kneaded with pine rosin, mastic, and wax into a stiff paste, wrapped in oiled cloth, then squeezed over a vessel. The first soft drops held the purest blue; each successive pressing gave a duller grade. Nothing was wasted, because nothing was affordable to waste.

And it was unaffordable. At various points ultramarine sold for more than gold, weight for weight. Painters' contracts began to read like insurance documents: patrons purchased the pigment themselves, kept it locked away, and doled it out under supervision. The Virgin Mary wears ultramarine in painting after painting not because the sky suggested her wardrobe but because doctrine ran on economics—the most precious color in the world belonged on the mother of God, and every worshipper understood the message without being told. Heaven, rendered in the substance that cost the most to obtain.

The expense broke even the mighty. Michelangelo walked away from his *Entombment* with the panel half-bare, and the story goes that the trouble was ultramarine—promised, undelivered, unpayable. When Vermeer died in Delft in 1675, he left his widow in debt, and biographers tracing his accounts have pointed to his pigment ledgers: he simply could not stop buying ultramarine. Consider what he spent it on—not only Mary's robes but a serving girl's apron, the turban of a girl with a pearl earring. He poured a fortune's worth of mountainside into ordinary women in ordinary rooms, which may be the most quietly radical act in the history of paint.

Then chemistry ruined everything, or rescued everything, depending on your sympathies. In the late 1820s, spurred by a French industry society's prize of six thousand francs, chemists cracked the recipe—a lattice of sodium aluminosilicate cooked with sulfur—and synthetic ultramarine flooded the market at a sliver of the price. Within decades the color that had outranked gold was pressed into laundry blocks and sold to housewives as bluing: a dab of sacred pigment in the washwater to cancel the yellowing of white cloth. The divine, demoted to detergent. You can decide for yourself whether that's a fall from grace or grace finally distributed.

Artists kept reaching for the synthetic anyway. In 1960, Yves Klein sealed a formula with France's patent office: ultramarine suspended in a clear resin that lets each particle glow unfiltered—the color he would use to paint sponges, models, entire rooms. He called it International Klein Blue and treated it less as a pigment than a state of mind. Chemists, meanwhile, had explained the original mystery: caged inside the mineral's crystal structure float chains of three sulfur atoms sharing one loose electron, a radical that swallows the long, warm wavelengths of light so thoroughly that the eye receives pure, bottomless blue. The medieval painters believed the stone contained something of heaven. They were wrong about the mechanism and right about the feeling.

What moves me most, though, is the endurance. Pigments die—alizarin madders fade to ghosts, copper greens corrode, lead white blackens in foul air—but ultramarine barely notices the centuries. The blue on those altarpieces is nearly the same blue that left the workshop, which means that standing before one, you are looking at something stranger than paint: a mountain in Afghanistan reduced to powder, carried on donkeys and galleys and ledger lines, squeezed drop by drop through oiled cloth, laid onto wood, and still burning. The sky made portable. Distance made visible.

Did blue mean heaven partly because it was difficult? I suspect so. Scarcity is a kind of argument; it insists that a thing matters, that someone climbed for it. Yet I cannot quite mourn the cheapness. Somewhere tonight a child smears French ultramarine across cheap paper with a stubby brush, owning outright what emperors once merely leased. The mines at Sar-e-Sang still operate; somewhere below the peaks, someone is still following the seam. Both truths stand at once: the color was once beyond price, and now it costs almost nothing, and neither fact has managed to exhaust it. Blue keeps its secret regardless of the invoice. It was never really about the money. The money was just the longest possible way of saying: *look.*

**In Between**

There is an hour that belongs to no one. It comes twice a day if you're paying attention—once when the night loosens its grip, once when it tightens again. Photographers call it the blue hour: that stretch after sunset or before sunrise when the sun sits below the horizon but its light still stains the upper atmosphere, and everything softens into a color most languages never bothered to name. It's too dark to work and too light to sleep. Nothing is required of you. The blue hour is a hinge, and lately I find myself drawn to hinges.

I've become interested in the in-between places, the ones we pass through so quickly we forget they exist. Consider the doorway. Architecture devotes enormous care to rooms—their purpose, their proportions, their light—but almost none to the few feet of transition between them. And yet ask anyone who has stood at a door, hand on the knob, suddenly unable to remember why they entered, and they'll tell you the threshold is not nothing. Psychologists have actually studied this: crossing a doorway seems to flush the mind, an event boundary that files the previous room's concerns away along with the previous room itself. The threshold doesn't just separate spaces. It edits us.

Or consider the hallway, which exists only to connect other places and is therefore furnished with everything we don't know what to do with: the coat rack, the mirror no one faces except in passing, the drawer of dead batteries and rubber bands and keys to locks long since replaced. Hallways are the honest parts of a house. They admit that most of life is transit.

Airports might be the great cathedrals of in-betweenness. Everyone there is suspended between departures and arrivals, legally nowhere, eating food that belongs to no cuisine, sleeping in postures that belong to no culture. Time behaves strangely in an airport. A three-hour layover can feel like an afternoon or a week depending entirely on whether your connecting flight exists yet. The airport is proof that human beings can survive, even function, in a state of pure postponement—that we can build whole temporary societies out of waiting.

Nature makes its own thresholds, and they are among its richest territories. The tide line, where the sea writes and rewrites its signature in foam and kelp and the shells of creatures that lived and died without witnesses. The estuary, where fresh water and salt meet in a brackish negotiation that supports more life than either side alone. The fog, which is simply a cloud that has come down to walk among us, turning every street into a corridor of possibility, hiding what's fifty feet away and making what's ten feet away luminous by contrast. Even the forest understands: ecologists will tell you the edge habitat, where woods give way to meadow, teems with more species than either the deep forest or the open field. Life concentrates at boundaries. This seems worth knowing beyond ecology.

We ourselves are made of thresholds. Adolescence is a decade-long border crossing with the paperwork constantly rejected. So is grief, which has no customs officer stamping you through; you stand in its terminal for however long it takes, holding luggage you cannot check. There is the strange country of convalescence, where you are too recovered to be ill and too changed to be well. There is the hypnagogic state, that dissolving minute before sleep when thoughts loosen their grammar and images arrive unbidden—a state so fertile that artists from Dalí to Edison tried deliberately to nap holding objects that would clang awake at the moment of entry, hoping to harvest whatever grew there.

Even language is a threshold technology. Every sentence is a ferry between two minds that will never actually touch, each word a small act of translation from the unspeakable interior to the audible exterior. Poetry lives hardest at this border—it is language leaning over the railing, trying to see the water.

What strikes me about all these in-between states is how badly we treat them. We are a civilization of destinations. Maps mark the cities, not the roads between them; calendars honor birthdays and anniversaries, not the unremarkable Tuesdays that constitute nearly all of life. We speak of waiting rooms, commutes, hallways, and layovers as time stolen from us, as obstacles between the real moments. The entire modern economy of efficiency is essentially a war on the threshold—an attempt to shrink the gap between wanting and having, question and answer, departure and arrival.

But the thresholds may be where the actual material of a life accumulates. Nobody remembers arriving at the beach; they remember the anticipation in the car, salt smell arriving through the window before the water did. Nobody's favorite memory of childhood is the birthday cake; it's lying awake the night before, listening to parents whispering downstairs, certain the wrapping paper sounds were sleigh bells. Anticipation, suspense, hesitation, the held breath—these aren't delays of experience. They are experience, in one of its purest forms.

So I've started practicing a small heresy: lingering at thresholds on purpose. Standing in doorways a beat longer than necessary. Taking the stairs slowly enough to notice the temperature change between floors. Watching dusk the way other people watch television—not to get anywhere, but because the getting-anywhere is happening regardless, and it's better company than I assumed. The blue hour lasts maybe half an hour. You cannot speed it up, and there is no app for it. It simply opens, hangs, and closes, twice a day, forever, whether or not anyone attends.

Perhaps that's the whole secret hiding in the in-between: nothing there is trying to sell us anything, hurry us anywhere, or make us into someone else. The threshold asks nothing. It just holds the door open—which, when you think about it, is one of the kindest gestures there is.

# The Extinction of Night

Night went extinct sometime in the last century, and nobody held a funeral.

If you consult a clock, of course, night still exists. The sun still sets on schedule. But ask yourself when you last stood in true darkness — not the dim amber murk of a streetlit neighborhood, not a bedroom with the curtains drawn against a glowing city, but darkness thick enough to erase your own hand when you wave it before your face. For most people alive today, the honest answer is *never*. Two-thirds of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. In North America, nearly four out of five people cannot see the Milky Way from their homes — not because clouds block it, but because we have painted it over with our own glow.

This would have struck our ancestors as an impossible sentence to write.

For almost the entire span of human history, night was a foreign country that ordinary people visited daily. It had its own geography, its own dangers, its own customs. And it shaped even something as intimate as sleep. Historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, medical texts, and court records going back centuries, discovered that before the modern era, people did not sleep in one long stretch. They slept in two segments — "first sleep" and "second sleep" — separated by an hour or more of quiet wakefulness around midnight. In that interval, people prayed, tended the fire, talked with family, visited neighbors, or simply lay thinking in the dark. The phrase "first sleep" appears across languages and continents; it wasn't a quirk, it was the default human rhythm, and artificial light quietly erased it within a few generations.

And what light it was. For millennia, after dark meant candle and hearth, rushlight and tallow smoke — expensive, feeble, flickering. The moon and stars weren't decoration; they were infrastructure. Farmers scheduled harvests by moonlight. Sailors steered by constellations. Travelers planned journeys around the phases of the moon the way we plan around traffic reports. The night sky was a clock, a compass, a calendar, and a scripture all at once, and everyone could read it.

Then came gaslight in the early 1800s, and cities learned to stay awake past sundown. Then Edison's lamp, then the grid, then everything. Within a century, night went from a frontier to a managed resource. Factories ran night shifts. Streets blazed all hours. Today, from orbit, the eastern United States, western Europe, Japan, and coastal China form continuous webs of light so bright that astronauts describe them as landmarks. We conquered the dark the way we conquered so much else — thoroughly, and without asking what we might be deleting.

Here is my favorite piece of evidence for what got deleted. When a powerful earthquake knocked out electricity across Los Angeles in 1994, worried residents called local emergency lines and observatories to report a strange phenomenon: a vast, glowing, silvery cloud stretched across the sky. Some suspected the earthquake had caused it. It was the Milky Way. They were seeing their own galaxy — the structure that contains every star anyone has ever seen with the naked eye — and mistaking it for an anomaly, because none of them had ever seen it before.

We tend to assume the losses are only aesthetic, a matter for poets and stargazers. They're not. Darkness is not an absence; it's a habitat. Roughly half of life's business happens in it. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from nests on beaches and instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the moon- and star-lit sea. Now beachfront resorts outshine the ocean, and thousands of hatchlings each season march inland, toward the lights, and die. Moths spiral helplessly into porch bulbs because they navigate by keeping a fixed angle to distant celestial lights — a strategy fine for the moon, fatal for a 60-watt filament. Migrating birds, which steer partly by the stars, collide with lit towers in staggering numbers. Fireflies flash their courtship signals into glare no mate can see. Even coral, spawning on cues from the lunar cycle, appear to falter under artificial skyglow. And in us: our bodies still run on the old clock. Light leaking into our evenings suppresses melatonin, delays sleep, scrambles rhythms calibrated over hundreds of thousands of nights.

What makes light pollution unusual among environmental wounds is that it is almost perfectly reversible. You cannot undo an oil spill by lunchtime. But switch off a town's lights, and the stars return that same night, undiminished, as if waiting patiently in the next room the whole while. Better fixtures that aim light down instead of up, warmer bulbs, sensors instead of all-night blaze — these cost little and restore an entire wilderness instantly. Darkness may be the last ecosystem we can resurrect with a timer.

But I'd argue the deepest loss is harder to tabulate. Stand under a genuinely dark sky — a high desert, a remote coast, one of the growing number of certified dark-sky reserves — and wait the twenty-some minutes it takes your eyes to rebuild their sensitivity. Then look up. The Milky Way is not a faint smudge, as photographs suggest. It is a luminous river, visibly structured, dramatic enough that ancient peoples across the world independently imagined it as a road of souls, spilled milk, a celestial serpent. Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* from his asylum window at Saint-Rémy, working partly from a sky he could actually still see. Most of us now paint our picture of the cosmos entirely from secondhand images.

Under that sky, something recalibrates. You can *feel* the Earth turning as the stars wheel slowly westward. You understand, in your body rather than in a textbook, that you are riding a planet through a galaxy, and that for nearly all of human history, every person you would ever have met knew exactly where they sat in that story, because they could look up and see it any clear night.

So consider this an invitation. Find some darkness while it survives — it clings to existence in pockets, patient and free. Bring a blanket, leave the phone face-down, and give your eyes time to do the ancient thing they were built to do. The night is still there. It has been waiting for us the whole time.

## The Keepers

Stand beneath a lighthouse after dark and wait. Every few seconds the beam swings past overhead — a brief white noon that lights the grass, the railing, your own hands — and then the dark returns, complete and unhurried, until the next pass. Five seconds. Seven. Each tower keeps its own interval, and once you know the pattern you can set your expectation by it, the way you learn the pace of a friend's footsteps on the stairs. This regularity was never decoration. It was the entire message: *I am here. I am still here. Count on me.*

For most of maritime history, a rocky shore at night was a lottery, and the sea held all the winning numbers. The first great English attempt to change this stood on the Eddystone reef, built by Henry Winstanley, an eccentric inventor who seems to have loved his improbable wooden tower the way people love impossible projects. When it was lit in 1698, he reportedly declared that he wished he might be aboard it during the worst storm England had ever seen, so he could watch it survive. In November 1703, he got his wish. The Great Storm flattened the tower and took him with it, making him, as far as anyone knows, the only engineer to die inside his own unfinished proof of concept.

It took a French physicist to make the idea survivable. In 1822, Augustin-Jean Fresnel assembled a lens that looked less like glasswork than like architecture: a central drum ringed by concentric panels of prisms, a beehive built to catch every stray ray of a single oil flame and bend it into one concentrated beam. Mounted first at Cordouan, near the mouth of the Gironde, it threw light twenty miles and more — from a fire smaller than a camp stove. Suddenly a keeper's little flame could argue with a gale across an entire horizon. In Scotland, an entire family, the Stevensons, devoted generations to raising these towers on black reefs; one of them, a frail young man named Robert Louis, was expected to join the firm and slipped away into fiction instead, though his books remained full of lights, islands, and signals sent into the dark.

The machinery that followed had a beautiful, honest clumsiness. The great lenses turned on baths of liquid mercury, driven by descending weights that keepers wound by hand, hour after hour, like tending an enormous grandfather clock. And because a sailor had to tell one light from another, each station was given a characteristic — a private signature written in flashes: two white bursts every ten seconds, a long eclipse, an occulting red. Navigators memorized them the way musicians memorize keys. The coastline became legible. A blur of terror resolved, flash by patient flash, into sentences you could read.

And so there grew up a profession whose entire purpose was attention. Keepers trimmed wicks, polished lenses, wound weights, scraped rust, and filled logbooks with entries of heroic mundanity: *wind moderate, visibility good, lamp burning well.* They painted the towers in bold bands so that sailors could read them by daylight too, and passed long rock-station exiles — three men to a light, months above the gray Atlantic — rationing conversation along with the coal. Occasionally the work turned legendary, as when Grace Darling, a keeper's daughter, rowed out through a wreck-strewn swell in 1838 to pull survivors from the *Forfarshire*; the deed shocked the nation partly because her ordinary life had been so quiet that any drama at all seemed miraculous. Mostly, though, the profession consisted of noticing things before they broke, and breaking nothing, ever. It was maintenance raised to the level of a vow.

Then came electricity, and after it the quiet arithmetic of automation. A sensor costs nothing per hour and sleeps through no storms. The lights converted one by one; by the end of 1998, Britain had closed its last staffed lighthouse. America held out longer: Boston Light, the country's oldest station, kept an actual resident keeper into this century — Sally Snowman, who tended it for nearly three decades before retiring in 2023, plausibly the last of her line. Nothing was gained except economy. What was lost is harder to enter into a ledger: the certainty that somewhere, through the whole black width of the night, a person was awake on your behalf.

We usually describe automation as the replacement of labor, but the lighthouse suggests it is also the retirement of vigilance — a specific, almost devotional form of watching. The keeper did not invent the light; engineers did that. The keeper guaranteed it. Their job was to stand between a promise and its failure. We still have such people — night nurses, controllers working the graveyard shift, the friend who answers the phone at three — but they are fewer than the dark requires, and their work is invisible by design. Constancy never photographs well. There is no dramatic moment in showing up every single time, and so we build fewer monuments to it than to almost anything else.

The lights themselves still turn. Solar panels feed them now; faults are relayed to offices far inland, and no one climbs the spiral stairs at midnight smelling of oil and rain. Yet on certain coasts the old beams still sweep across the water like slow sentences repeated to the dark, on schedule, exactly as advertised. Standing under one, counting the seconds, I find that is as serviceable a definition of love as any: not intensity, which burns out, but cadence — the promise made small enough to keep forever, and then kept. The beam passes. You lose sight of everything. The beam returns.

*I am here. I am still here. Count on me.*

# In Praise of the Dark

For nearly all of human history, nightfall was less an inconvenience than a border crossing. When the sun went down, people didn't simply dim—they migrated into a different country with its own rules, sounds, dangers, and freedoms. The night belonged to owls and thieves, to lovers and ghosts, to the watchman's tread and the wolf's call. To imagine what darkness once meant, you have to subtract every glowing screen, every streetlamp, every humble porch light. You have to imagine a world where, after sunset, the brightest thing visible might be the moon—or nothing at all but the faint river of the Milky Way spilling across the sky.

Artificial light arrived slowly, then all at once. For millennia we burned whatever we could: pinewood splinters, rushes dipped in grease, olive oil, tallow, beeswax reserved for churches and the wealthy. By the eighteenth century, whole industries rose and fell on the hunt for illumination—most famously the whaling fleets that chased spermaceti and whale oil across oceans, killing tens of thousands of animals so that respectable homes could stay lit a few hours longer. Gaslight came to city streets in the early 1800s, and then, in 1879, Edison's practical incandescent bulb quietly ended the ten-thousand-year reign of flame. Within a single century, night became optional. Humanity performed one of its greatest magic tricks: we abolished the dark, and almost nobody noticed the disappearance.

But something was lost in the trick, and historians have been recovering its outlines. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, letters, medical texts, and old ballads, and he found evidence that before the modern era, people in many cultures did not sleep through the night the way we do. They slept in two segments. After a "first sleep" lasting several hours, they would wake naturally around midnight and enter a quiet, contemplative interval—a hour or two of prayer, conversation, reading by candle, lovemaking, or simply lying awake while the household breathed around them. Then came the "second sleep" until dawn. Writers described this waking as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world, a soft intermission built into human biology. It suggests that our idea of one seamless eight-hour night is not an ancient truth but a recent invention, made possible—and perhaps enforced—by electric light.

Consider what the night sky itself once was. Today, according to studies of global light pollution, a third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, including the majority of people in North America and Europe. Most of us look up and see a handful of hardy stars struggling through the glow. But for our ancestors, the sky was a dense archive. Every culture projected its stories up there—the hunter and the bear, the river of souls, the emu made of darkness between the stars rather than the stars themselves. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific reading star paths, swells, and the behavior of birds, holding entire hemispheres of sky in memory like maps. Farmers timed harvests by constellations. The night sky was humanity's first calendar, first scripture, first GPS—and within living memory, we have largely misplaced it.

Yet darkness is not emptiness, and the natural world never got the memo about our lights. In the open ocean, below the last reach of sunlight, life makes its own radiance. Roughly three quarters of deep-sea creatures are bioluminescent: anglerfish dangling lures of glowing bacteria, jellyfish pulsing blue-green alarms, tiny copepods vomiting light when disturbed so that larger predators can see their attackers—and retaliate. Fireflies synchronize by the thousands in forests of Southeast Asia, flashing in waves of collective rhythm no individual insect understands. Fungi glow in rainforests to lure insects that spread their spores. Even the waves themselves can burn neon blue when plankton are agitated, so that surfers wading in at midnight trail light behind them like falling angels. Darkness, it turns out, is full of conversation. We just stopped speaking the language.

And here is the strangest thought of all: darkness isn't merely common—it's fundamental. Everything we can see, everything made of atoms that shine, reflect, or burn, accounts for less than five percent of the universe. The rest is dark: dark matter holding galaxies together with unseen gravity, and dark energy pulling the cosmic expansion ever faster, both utterly mysterious. The luminous universe—the whole glittering show of stars, nebulae, and galaxies—is a thin bright skin stretched over an ocean of dark. Light is the exception. Darkness is the rule. When we flood the night with glare, we may be blinding ourselves twice over: once to the stars above, and once to the deeper fact that the universe's true nature is hidden from us, patient, waiting for better eyes.

There are quieter losses, too. Our bodies still keep ancient time. Darkness prompts the release of melatonin, coordinating sleep, immune function, and countless cellular repairs; chronic exposure to light at night scrambles these rhythms in ways linked to poor sleep and worse health. More than a hundred years of electric night has been called, only half-jokingly, the largest experiment in human biology ever conducted without informed consent. Meanwhile, sea turtle hatchlings, which instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon of the moonlit sea, die in droves on developed beaches because they crawl instead toward the sodium glow of highway lights. Migrating birds circle illuminated skyscrapers until they drop. We are only beginning to tally the bill.

So consider darkness not as absence but as a presence worth seeking—one of the few remaining wildernesses left, and one you don't have to travel far to visit. Drive past the edge of the suburbs on a clear, moonless night and turn off your headlights for a moment. Give your eyes half an hour; they will open like flowers. Then look up, find the faint gray smear of the Milky Way, and remember: you are standing inside a galaxy of four hundred billion suns, seeing it edge-on from the arm of an ordinary spiral, under a sky your ancestors knew intimately and you may be meeting for the very first time. The dark was never the enemy. It is the original context, the resting place, the vast honest backdrop against which every light—every star, every firefly, every small burning human idea—actually means something. Turn off the lamp. See what remains.

# Everything Arrives Late

Every child who counts the seconds between lightning and thunder has performed the oldest experiment in the universe's bureaucracy. One Mississippi, two Mississippi, three—and there it is: the discovery that distance means delay, that the world does not report to us instantly, that even catastrophe arrives by slow post.

We never quite recover from this. Moonlight is 1.3 seconds old when it touches your face. Sunlight is eight minutes stale—every tan and every sunbeam is news from the recent past. Step outside on a clear night and the delay becomes geological. Sirius is eight years away. Betelgeuse, hundreds. If it detonated tonight, astronomers would keep describing its steady red glow for centuries, updating us faithfully on the health of a corpse.

And then there's Andromeda, the faint smudge visible on autumn nights just past the edge of seeing. Its light has traveled 2.5 million years to arrive in your retina—which means it left roughly when our ancestors were first striking flakes off stones. When you find it in the sky, you are looking at a message sent before anyone existed to read it.

But here's the part that unsettles me more: the slowness doesn't stop at your skin. Sound crosses a room in milliseconds. Nerve impulses crawl at a finite speed. The brain receives its dispatches—sight, sound, touch—at different rates and then quietly edits them into a single synchronized broadcast. Some experiments suggest that what we experience as *now* was assembled a fraction of a second after the fact. The present, in other words, is not a window. It's a newsroom. Somewhere behind your eyes, an editor is stitching together a coherent story from footage that arrived late, smoothing over the gaps, and stamping it LIVE.

So we live perpetually in the recent past, reading yesterday's edition of the universe and calling it today.

And yet—I've come to find this consoling rather than sad. Because a universe with built-in delay is a universe that keeps records. Nothing that shines vanishes outright; its light keeps traveling, faithful and undelivered, sometimes for billions of years. Point a telescope anywhere and you're not looking at space, exactly. You're looking backward through the archive. Push far enough and you reach the cosmic microwave background—the oldest surviving broadcast, the static hissed out when the universe was young and hot and everything was fog. Astronomers are, professionally speaking, historians with better equipment.

Which brings me to the smallest case, and my favorite. Sit across a table from someone you love. The light leaving their face takes a few nanoseconds to reach you—a delay so trivial no clock bothers with it, but nonzero nonetheless. You have never once seen anyone in the present tense. Not your mother, not your child, not the stranger who smiled at you on the train. Everyone you've ever known, you've known strictly through the past.

All love, technically, is nostalgia.

Maybe that's why the delay exists. Not as a flaw in the design, but as the universe's way of insisting that nothing real ever ends abruptly—that every moment, once lived, keeps moving outward forever, arriving somewhere, eventually, at someone who will receive it and call it beautiful.

**On Marginalia**

There's a medieval manuscript in a Dutch library where a scribe, somewhere around the year 1200, complained in the margin that his ink was freezing and his fingers were too cold to hold the quill. Another scribe, finishing a long copying job, wrote at the bottom of the final page: *"Now I've done it, but my hand will remember this for a long time."* And one simply noted, next to an elaborate illustration: *"A cat peed on this page. May God punish it."*

I love these things more than almost anything else in the historical record. Not the treaties, not the chronicles of kings — the complaints about cold hands. Because a treaty tells you what powerful people wanted posterity to believe. A margin note tells you that someone, eight hundred years ago, had a bad day exactly like you have bad days, and got annoyed about it in precisely the way you'd get annoyed.

Used bookstore copies carry the same electricity. Someone in 1974 underlined a passage in a paperback novel and wrote *YES!!* in the margin, and now you're reading it, decades later, and you either feel a jolt of agreement — a stranger nodding at you across time — or you disagree, and you're arguing with a ghost who can never defend themselves. Either way, a conversation has occurred between two people who will never meet, mediated by paper.

We tend to think of writing as a technology for transmitting information, but margins are evidence of its other function entirely: writing as a place where a self can leave fingerprints. The main text is the message. The marginalia is the messenger leaking through.

There's something quietly consoling about this. We assume that being remembered requires significance — achievements, monuments, names carved in stone. But the actual record suggests otherwise. What survives, improbably, is the trivial and the true. The monk's cold hands outlived the abbot he worked for. The cat's crime is now immortal.

So maybe the lesson is this: if you want to be known by the future, don't try to be important. Try to be honest about something small. Complain about the weather. Admit you were tired. Write *YES!!* in a book you loved.

Some future reader, thumbing through whatever remains of us, won't remember the official version of any of this era anyway. They'll remember the note in the margin — because that's where the living actually are.
